stages.title: Physical measurements and SI units
stages.hook: Two friends measure the same table: one says '5 hand-spans', the other says '6'. Who is right, and how could they agree?
explain: To share results, scientists measure with agreed units. The international system is called SI. Its base units include the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass and the second (s) for time.
Prefixes make units bigger or smaller: kilo means ×1000, centi means ÷100 and milli means ÷1000. So 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 m = 1000 mm.
Every measurement has some uncertainty, because instruments have limits. We write a number with its unit, and we choose a sensible instrument: a ruler for a pencil, a measuring tape for a room.

example.q: A rope is 2.5 km long. How many metres is that?

analogies.home: A recipe asks for 250 g of flour. If everyone used different cups, the cake would differ each time.
analogies.city: Road signs in km and shops selling kg work because everybody uses the same units.
analogies.sport: A 100 m race is the same distance in every country, so records can be compared.
analogies.tech: A phone screen shows storage in gigabytes, a standard everyone agrees on.

stages.mnemonic: Metre, kilogram, second: the three base units that start the SI line.
terms: The international system of units used in science.
A word-start such as kilo or milli that scales a unit.
How far a measurement might be from the true value.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kg.

misc.wrong: A measurement is just a number.
misc.right: A measurement needs a number and a unit, and it always has some uncertainty.

stages.limits: SI is a human agreement, not a law of nature. Other units, such as miles, are still used in some places and must be converted.

trip.prompt: Find the seven SI base units and the quantity each one measures.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.why: Mass is measured in kilograms. Newtons measure force and metres measure length.

questions.q: Which unit would you use to measure the length of a classroom?
questions.why: Length is measured in metres.

questions.q: Convert 3.2 kilometres into metres.
A pencil is 175 mm long. How long is it in centimetres?
A bag has a mass of 2500 g. What is its mass in kilograms?
What does the prefix 'milli' mean?
questions.why: Milli means ÷1000, so a millimetre is one thousandth of a metre.

questions.q: Match each quantity to its SI base unit.
questions.why: These are three of the seven SI base units.

questions.q: Two students time a toy car over 2 m: 3.1 s and 3.3 s. Why might the results differ?
o: One student is wrong and must be punished
questions.why: Reaction time and instrument limits cause small differences. Repeating and averaging helps.

questions.q: Why do scientists in different countries use the same units?
questions.model: Using the same standard units lets scientists compare and share results without confusion.
questions.why: Agreed units remove ambiguity, so results can be compared.

questions.q: A recipe uses 0.5 kg of rice. A student weighs 5000 g. Which is true?
o: There is ten times too much
The amounts match because 0.5 and 5000 are close
There is half the amount needed
There is ten times too little
questions.why: 0.5 kg = 500 g, and 5000 g is ten times 500 g.

panel.q: A ruler shows marks every 1 mm. A student reports a length of 12.3456 cm. What is wrong?
o: The reading is more precise than the ruler allows
Centimetres cannot be used to measure a length
A ruler cannot be used to measure a length at all
The reading should have been given as a negative number
panel.why: A ruler marked in mm can be read to about 0.5 mm, so reporting four decimals claims impossible precision.

panel.q: Why can a bare number such as '12' be a poor answer in science?
panel.model: Without a unit, 12 could mean 12 metres, seconds or kilograms. The unit gives the number its meaning.
panel.why: A quantity is a number times a unit.

panel.q: Which measurement has the largest value?
panel.why: 0.002 km is 2 m. The others are 1.5 m, 1.8 m and 1.2 m.

teach.topic: Why we use SI units and prefixes
teach.model: Scientists use the same units so everyone gets the same answer for the same thing. The metre measures length, the kilogram mass and the second time. Prefixes like kilo (×1000) and milli (÷1000) change the size. For example, 2 km is 2000 m.

points.ask: What is a unit and why do we need one?
Why should everyone use the same one?
What do kilo and milli mean?
Can you give me an example with a number?

stages.title: Distance, displacement, speed and time
stages.hook: A runner does one full lap of a 400 m track and ends where she started. How far did she run, and how far is she from the start?
explain: Distance is the total length of the path travelled. Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, with a direction. After one full lap the distance is 400 m but the displacement is zero.
Speed tells how fast something moves: speed = distance ÷ time. In SI the unit is metres per second (m/s). To change km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.
A distance-time graph shows motion: a steep line means fast, a flat line means stopped, and a straight sloping line means steady speed. Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.

example.q: A cyclist rides 30 km in 2 hours. What is the average speed?

analogies.city: A taxi drives around the block and stops at its start. The meter counts distance, but the displacement is zero.
analogies.sport: A 400 m runner finishes where she began, so the displacement is zero although she covered 400 m.
analogies.sea: A ferry sails 10 km east and 10 km back. The distance is 20 km, the displacement is zero.
analogies.tech: A phone map shows total route length (distance) and the direct line between points (displacement).

stages.mnemonic: Distance is the path walked; displacement is the arrow from start to end.
terms: Total length of the path travelled.
Straight-line change in position, with direction.
Total distance divided by total time.

misc.wrong: Distance and displacement are always the same.
misc.right: They are equal only for straight-line travel in one direction. Displacement can even be zero after a long trip.

stages.limits: Average speed hides changes: a car can be at 0 km/h and at 100 km/h during a trip with a 50 km/h average.

trip.prompt: Find how speed and velocity differ in the article.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of speed?
questions.why: Speed is distance over time: m/s.

questions.q: A train travels 240 km in 3 hours at a steady rate. What is its speed?
A sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s. What is the average speed?
How long, in seconds, does a bus moving at 12 m/s take to travel 600 m?
questions.why: time = distance ÷ speed = 600 ÷ 12 = 50 s.

questions.q: Convert 72 km/h into m/s. Divide by 3.6.
A child walks 3 m east then 3 m west back to the start. What is the displacement?
questions.why: She ends at the starting point, so her change in position is zero. The distance is 6 m.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, what does a flat horizontal line mean?
questions.why: The distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest.

questions.q: Order these speeds from slowest to fastest.
questions.why: These typical values increase in the order shown.

questions.q: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the second hour. Explain how to find its average speed.
questions.model: Add the distances to get 100 km, add the times to get 2 h, then divide: 100 ÷ 2 = 50 km/h.
questions.why: Average speed uses total distance over total time, not the mean of anything else.

questions.q: A car goes 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 60 km/h. Is the average speed 45 km/h?
questions.why: Time = 2 h + 1 h = 3 h for 120 km, so 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h. The slower part takes longer.

panel.q: A marathon runner finishes 42.2 km from where she started, on a looping route. Which is true?
o: Her distance is 42.2 km but her displacement could be much smaller
Her displacement must also be 42.2 km
Her displacement must be exactly zero because she moved
Her distance and displacement are always equal
panel.why: Distance follows the path; displacement is the straight-line change in position, which depends on where the loop ends.

panel.q: Why can a car's speedometer read 90 km/h when its average speed over the trip was only 50 km/h?
panel.model: The speedometer shows speed at one instant. The average divides total distance by total time, which includes slower parts and stops.
panel.why: Average speed smooths over changes in speed.

panel.q: A distance-time graph is a straight line that slopes steeply upwards. What does that tell you?
panel.why: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed. Steep and straight means large and constant.

teach.topic: The difference between distance and displacement, and how to find speed
teach.model: Distance is how far you travelled along your path. Displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish with a direction. Speed is distance divided by time. For example, walking 100 m in 50 s is 2 m/s.

points.ask: What is distance?
How is displacement different?
How do I work out speed?
Can you give me an example with numbers?

stages.title: Forces and Newton's laws
stages.hook: A parent pushes an empty buggy and a loaded one with the same effort. Which one speeds up more, and what law explains it?
explain: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). Forces have a size and a direction. When forces on an object are balanced, its motion does not change: it stays at rest or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line. This is Newton's first law.
When forces are unbalanced, the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force. Newton's second law: F = m × a, where F is in newtons, m in kilograms and a in m/s².
Newton's third law: when object A pushes on object B, B pushes back on A with an equal force in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other.

example.q: A 60 N resultant force pushes a 15 kg crate. What is its acceleration?
steps: Write F = m × a, so a = F ÷ m.

analogies.farm: A donkey pulls an empty cart easily. Load it with sacks and the same pull gives a slower start.
analogies.sport: A rower pushes water backwards with the oar and the boat moves forwards.
analogies.sea: A small boat and a big ship, pushed by the same wind, speed up very differently.
analogies.tech: A rocket pushes hot gas downwards, and the gas pushes the rocket upwards.

stages.mnemonic: First: balance means no change. Second: F = m a. Third: forces come in pairs.
terms: A push or pull, measured in newtons (N).
The single force that has the same effect as all forces combined.
An object's resistance to a change in motion.
Rate of change of velocity, in m/s².

misc.wrong: A moving object must have a force acting on it in the direction it moves.
misc.right: A force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going. Friction is usually what slows objects down.

stages.limits: These laws describe everyday speeds and sizes. Near the speed of light or inside atoms we need relativity and quantum physics.

trip.prompt: Find an example from space travel for each of the three laws.

questions.q: A hockey puck slides on very smooth ice and travels far. What does this show?
o: With little friction, motion hardly changes
Moving things always need a constant push to go on
questions.why: With very little friction there is almost no resultant force, so the puck keeps its speed.

questions.q: A resultant force of 30 N acts on a 6 kg trolley. What is its acceleration?
What resultant force gives a 1200 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
A 10 N resultant force acts on an object and gives it an acceleration of 4 m/s². What is its mass in kg?
Two teams pull a rope with 400 N each in opposite directions and the rope does not move. What is the resultant force?
questions.why: Equal and opposite forces cancel, so the resultant is zero and the rope stays at rest.

questions.q: A skater pushes off a wall. Why does she move away?
o: The wall pushes back on her
The wall pushes her away because it has more mass
Gravity is switched off for a moment
questions.why: By the third law, her push on the wall is matched by an equal push from the wall on her.

questions.q: Match each situation to the law that best explains it.
pairs: A tablecloth is pulled quickly and the cups stay
A heavier trolley is harder to speed up
A balloon rushes away as air escapes
questions.why: Each example shows one law most clearly.

questions.q: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road and gradually slows down. Which forces cause this, and what does it say about Newton's first law?
questions.model: Friction and air resistance act against the motion, so the forces are unbalanced and the speed changes. Without them the cyclist would keep going at a steady speed.
questions.why: Slowing is evidence of an unbalanced force; the first law says motion would otherwise stay the same.

questions.q: A car moves at a steady 15 m/s in a straight line. Which statement is correct?
o: The resultant force on it is zero
It has no forces at all
questions.why: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the forces balance.

questions.q: The same force acts on a 2 kg box and a 4 kg box. What is the ratio of their accelerations (2 kg : 4 kg)?
questions.why: a = F ÷ m, so the lighter box has twice the acceleration.

panel.q: A student says: 'In a tug of war the winning team pulls harder on the losing team than the losing team pulls back.' What is the best reply?
o: The pulls are equal; the winners push harder on the ground and friction decides
She is right, and the winners simply pull harder on the rope
The rope itself decides who wins the contest
Winners always have more inertia than losers
panel.why: The two pulls on the rope are equal and opposite. Winning depends on the friction forces from the ground on each team.

panel.q: An astronaut floats in a spacecraft and pushes a heavy box. Explain what happens to the astronaut and the box.
panel.model: The box pushes back on the astronaut with an equal force, so both move in opposite directions. The one with less mass accelerates more.
panel.why: Newton's third law gives equal forces, and the second law gives different accelerations for different masses.

panel.q: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s² along a floor, and friction is 4 N. What is the pulling force?
panel.why: Resultant = 2 × 3 = 6 N. The pull must beat friction too: 6 + 4 = 10 N.

teach.topic: Why a heavy trolley is harder to speed up
teach.model: A force is a push or pull. The resultant force makes an object accelerate, and a bigger mass means a smaller acceleration for the same force. That is F = m × a. For example, 10 N on a 2 kg trolley gives 5 m/s², but on a 5 kg trolley it gives only 2 m/s².

points.ask: What is a force?
Why does mass matter?
What does the force actually change?
Is there a rule or an example with numbers?

stages.title: Gravity and weight
stages.hook: On the Moon an astronaut can jump much higher. Does the astronaut have less stuff in their body there, or something else changed?
explain: Gravity is a pull between all objects that have mass. Near a planet it pulls things towards the planet's centre. Mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kilograms. Weight is the gravitational force on an object, measured in newtons.
Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g). On Earth's surface g is about 9.8 N/kg, often rounded to 10. On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so the same object weighs about one sixth as much.
Mass does not change from place to place, but weight does. In free fall without air, all objects accelerate at the same rate, about 9.8 m/s² on Earth.

example.q: A 5 kg backpack is on Earth. What is its weight? Use g = 9.8 N/kg.

analogies.home: A bag of rice has the same amount of rice anywhere, but it feels lighter when carried on the Moon.
analogies.sport: A high jumper reaches a greater height on the Moon because gravity pulls less.
analogies.tech: A bathroom scale measures the push upward on you, which is your weight, and then displays kg by assuming Earth's g.

stages.mnemonic: Mass is stuff, weight is the pull: W = m g.
terms: The attractive force between objects with mass.
The gravitational force on an object, in newtons.
How much matter an object contains, in kg.
Force per kilogram, g, about 9.8 N/kg on Earth.

misc.wrong: Mass and weight are the same thing.
misc.right: Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same. Weight is a force that depends on gravity.

stages.limits: We treat g as constant near the surface. It decreases with height and varies slightly across Earth, from about 9.78 to 9.83 N/kg.

trip.prompt: Find a table of g on the Moon, Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of weight?
questions.why: Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons.

questions.q: What is the weight of a 3 kg book on Earth? Use g = 10 N/kg.
An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg. What is her weight on the Moon where g = 1.6 N/kg?
An object weighs 98 N on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). What is its mass?
A rock is taken from Earth to the Moon. What happens?
o: Its mass stays the same and its weight decreases
Its mass decreases and its weight stays the same
Both its mass and weight decrease on the Moon
Both its mass and weight stay the same
questions.why: Mass is amount of matter, which is unchanged. Weight depends on g, which is smaller on the Moon.

questions.q: In a vacuum chamber a feather and a hammer are dropped together. What happens?
o: They land at the same time
The hammer lands first because it is heavier
The feather lands first because it is lighter
Neither one falls without air to push it
questions.why: Without air resistance, all objects have the same acceleration due to gravity.

questions.q: Order these places by gravitational field strength at the surface, from lowest to highest.
questions.why: The Moon is smallest, then Mars, Earth and Jupiter, which is larger.

questions.q: Match each quantity to its unit.
questions.why: Mass in kilograms, weight (a force) in newtons, field strength in newtons per kilogram.

questions.q: Explain why an astronaut has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth but a different weight.
questions.model: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. Weight is the pull of gravity, which is smaller on the Moon, so her weight is smaller.
questions.why: Weight = mass × g, and g differs between places.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball falls freely in a vacuum and a 6 kg ball also falls freely. Which statement is correct?
o: The 6 kg ball accelerates 3 times faster
The 2 kg ball accelerates 3 times faster
questions.why: Weight is 3 times bigger for 6 kg, but so is the mass, so a = W ÷ m = g for both.

panel.q: A student claims, 'There is no gravity in the space station, that is why astronauts float.' What is the best correction?
o: Gravity there is still about 90% of that on Earth; they float because they are in free fall around Earth
She is right, since gravity ends a few hundred km above the ground
Gravity is switched off by the thick walls of the station
Astronauts float because they lose most of their mass in orbit
panel.why: At a height of about 400 km gravity is still around 90% of surface value. The station and astronauts are falling together around Earth.

panel.q: Would a bathroom scale that is calibrated on Earth show the right mass on the Moon? Explain.
panel.model: No. The scale really measures the force pressing on it, which is smaller on the Moon, so it would show only about one sixth of the true mass.
panel.why: Scales measure weight and convert it to mass using Earth's g.

panel.q: A 60 kg person has a weight of about 588 N on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). What is their weight where g = 3.7 N/kg?

teach.topic: The difference between mass and weight
teach.model: Mass is how much matter something has, measured in kilograms, and it stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity on it, measured in newtons, and it changes from planet to planet. Weight = mass × g. For example, a 10 kg object weighs about 98 N on Earth but only 16 N on the Moon.

points.ask: What is mass?
What is weight?
Why does weight change but mass does not?
How do I work it out? Can you show an example?

stages.title: Work, energy and power
stages.hook: Lifting a box up one step and lifting it up ten steps both need effort. How can we measure how much, and how fast it is done?
explain: In physics, work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: work = force × distance. The unit is the joule (J). Energy is the ability to do work and is also measured in joules.

Energy comes in forms: kinetic (movement), gravitational potential (height), thermal, chemical, electrical and more. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Kinetic energy = ½ × m × v², and gravitational potential energy near Earth = m × g × h.
Power is the rate of doing work: power = energy ÷ time. The unit is the watt (W), which is one joule per second. Efficiency tells what fraction of the input energy becomes useful output.

example.q: A girl lifts a 20 N bag up 2 m in 4 s. How much work is done and what is the power?

analogies.farm: Carrying a sack up a ramp takes work; doing it quickly needs more power.
analogies.sport: A weightlifter does work on the barbell; a sprinter shows high power by working fast.
analogies.city: A lift (elevator) with a stronger motor lifts people to the top floor faster: same work, more power.
analogies.tech: A 60 W bulb transfers 60 joules of energy every second.

stages.mnemonic: Work is force times distance; power is how fast the work happens.
terms: Energy transferred when a force moves something, in joules.
Energy transferred per second, in watts.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input.

misc.wrong: Energy gets used up and disappears.
misc.right: Energy is conserved. It is transferred and often spread out as heat, which makes it less useful.

stages.limits: The simple formula work = force × distance applies when the force is along the direction of motion. Real machines always lose some energy as heat.

trip.prompt: List the forms of energy shown in the article and find one example of each.

questions.q: What is the unit of power?
questions.why: Power is measured in watts, equal to joules per second.

questions.q: A force of 50 N pushes a box 3 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
A machine does 600 J of work in 12 s. What is its power?
What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg book 3 m above the floor? Use g = 10 N/kg.
What is the kinetic energy of a 4 kg ball moving at 5 m/s? Use KE = ½ m v².
A lamp takes in 100 J of electrical energy and gives out 20 J of light. What is the efficiency?
questions.why: Efficiency = useful output ÷ input = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. The rest becomes heat.

questions.q: Match the energy form to an example.
pairs: A book on a high shelf
questions.why: Each example stores or shows a different form of energy.

questions.q: Order the energy changes in a hydroelectric plant.
items: Gravitational potential energy of water in the dam
Kinetic energy of a turning turbine
questions.why: Water falls, the turbine spins and the generator makes electricity.

questions.q: Two people carry identical 30 kg bags up the same stairs. One takes 20 s and the other takes 40 s. Who does more work and who has more power?
questions.model: They do the same work, because the force and the height are the same. The person who takes 20 s has twice the power because the same work is done in half the time.
questions.why: Work depends on force and distance only, but power also depends on time.

questions.q: A ball is thrown upwards, rises, then falls. At its highest point, which statement is correct?
o: Gravitational potential energy is greatest and kinetic energy is least
Kinetic energy is greatest and potential energy is least
All its energy has disappeared for a moment
questions.why: At the top, the ball is momentarily slowest and highest, so potential energy is maximum.

panel.q: A student holds a heavy box still for one minute and is tired. How much work in the physics sense is done on the box?
o: None, because the box does not move
A lot, because holding a heavy box takes effort
An amount equal to the weight of the box
An amount equal to the mass of the box
panel.why: Work needs movement in the direction of the force. Muscles still use energy internally.

panel.q: A claim says: 'A machine is 120% efficient, so it makes extra energy.' Explain why this cannot be true.
panel.model: Energy is conserved, so the useful output can never exceed the input. Efficiency is always below 100% because some energy is wasted as heat and sound.
panel.why: More output than input would break the conservation of energy.

panel.q: If a car's speed doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?
o: It halves, to half as large
panel.why: KE = ½ m v², so doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4.

teach.topic: The difference between work, energy and power
teach.model: Energy is the ability to do work and is measured in joules. Work is done when a force moves something: force times distance. Power is how fast work is done, in watts. For example, lifting a 20 N bag 2 m takes 40 J, and doing it in 4 s is 10 W.

points.ask: What is energy?
What do we mean by work?
And what is power?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Matter, density and pressure
stages.hook: A huge steel ship floats, but a tiny steel nail sinks. How can that be?
explain: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space. It exists as solid, liquid or gas. In solids the particles are tightly packed and vibrate in place, in liquids they slide past one another, and in gases they move freely and far apart.

Density tells how much mass is packed into a volume: density = mass ÷ volume. The unit is kg/m³ (water is about 1000 kg/m³). An object floats in a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid, on average.

Pressure is force spread over an area: pressure = force ÷ area. The unit is the pascal (Pa), which is 1 N per m². The same force on a small area gives a bigger pressure, which is why a knife is sharp.

example.q: A block has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 250 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
steps: Density is 2 g/cm³, which is more than water (1 g/cm³), so it sinks.

analogies.sea: A ship is hollow and full of air, so its average density is less than water and it floats.
analogies.home: Wearing snowshoes spreads your weight over a bigger area, so you do not sink.
analogies.nature: A camel's wide feet spread its weight so it can walk on sand.
analogies.farm: A tractor with wide tyres presses less on soft ground.

stages.mnemonic: Density: pack of mass in a box. Pressure: force over footprint.
terms: Force per unit area, in pascals.
The space an object takes up.
A tiny piece of matter such as an atom or molecule.

misc.wrong: Heavy things always sink and light things always float.
misc.right: Floating depends on density, not just weight. A huge ship floats and a small pebble sinks.

stages.limits: The particle picture of three states is simple. Plasma is a fourth state, and some materials like glass or gels do not fit neatly.

trip.prompt: Find a table of densities and see where water, wood and iron appear.

questions.q: In which state of matter are the particles closest together and held in place?
questions.why: Solid particles are tightly packed and only vibrate.

questions.q: A rock has a mass of 300 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density?
A force of 200 N acts on an area of 0.5 m². What is the pressure?
questions.why: Pressure = 200 ÷ 0.5 = 400 Pa.

questions.q: What mass of water fills a 2 m³ tank? Use density 1000 kg/m³.
questions.why: Mass = density × volume = 1000 × 2 = 2000 kg.

questions.q: A wooden block has a density of 600 kg/m³. Will it float in water (1000 kg/m³)?
o: Yes, because it is less dense
No, because wood is a solid material
No, because water is a heavy liquid
Only if the block is very small
questions.why: An object less dense than the liquid floats.

questions.q: Why does a nail go into wood point first rather than head first?
o: The small point area gives a large pressure
The point is heavier than the head
The head is lighter than the point
The point has more mass than the head
questions.why: Same force over a small area gives much higher pressure.

questions.q: Match each state to its particle description.
questions.why: Particle arrangement explains the properties of each state.

questions.q: Order these from least dense to most dense.
questions.why: Air is about 1.2 kg/m³, wood several hundred, water 1000 and iron about 7900 kg/m³.

questions.q: Explain why a steel ship floats although steel is denser than water.
questions.model: The ship's hull is hollow and holds a lot of air, so its average density, steel and air together, is less than water. It displaces enough water to support its weight.
questions.why: Floating depends on average density.

questions.q: A 60 kg person stands on two feet with a total area of 0.04 m². Take weight = 600 N. What is the pressure on the ground?

panel.q: A cube of iron and a cube of foam have exactly the same mass. Which statement must be true?
panel.why: Same mass with lower density means larger volume.

panel.q: Why do we wear snowshoes to walk on deep snow?
panel.model: Snowshoes spread our weight over a larger area, which lowers the pressure on the snow, so we sink less.
panel.why: Pressure = force ÷ area, so a bigger area means lower pressure.

panel.q: A piece of ice floats in water. What does this tell us about ice?
o: It is less dense than liquid water
It is more dense than liquid water
It has no mass at all
It has exactly the same density as steel
panel.why: Ice has a density of about 920 kg/m³, a little less than water, so it floats.

teach.topic: What density is and why some things float
teach.model: Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume: mass divided by volume. Things less dense than water float, and things more dense sink. For example, wood floats but iron sinks because iron packs more mass in the same space.

points.ask: What do you mean by density?
How do I calculate it?
How does that decide floating?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Heat and temperature
stages.hook: A small cup of boiling water and a bathtub of warm water: which holds more heat energy, and which has the higher temperature?
explain: Temperature measures how hot something is, in terms of the average kinetic energy of its particles. It is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K). Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules.

Heat moves in three ways. Conduction passes energy through direct contact, mostly in solids like metals. Convection carries energy in moving liquids and gases. Radiation sends energy as infrared waves and needs no material, which is how the Sun warms Earth.

Heating usually makes things expand slightly. Adding heat changes temperature or, at melting and boiling, changes state. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal sea-level pressure. Kelvin = Celsius + 273.

analogies.home: A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot by conduction; the soup itself swirls by convection.
analogies.sea: Warm sea water rises and cool water sinks, making currents.
analogies.nature: A rock in sunshine warms by radiation.
analogies.city: Radiators near the floor warm a room as the warm air rises.

stages.mnemonic: Conduction touches, convection circulates, radiation travels.
terms: A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles.
Energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
Heat transfer by the movement of fluids.

misc.wrong: Heat and temperature are the same.
misc.right: Temperature says how hot; heat is energy that flows. A bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a cup of hotter water.

stages.limits: Everyday ideas use 'cold' as if it flowed, but physics describes only heat flowing from hot to cold. Real materials differ in how well they conduct.

trip.prompt: Find a picture for each of conduction, convection and radiation.

questions.q: Which way does heat flow between two objects in contact?
o: From the hotter to the colder
From the colder to the hotter
From the heavier to the lighter
questions.why: Heat flows from higher to lower temperature.

questions.q: Convert 37 °C to kelvin. Use K = °C + 273.
Convert 300 K to degrees Celsius. Use °C = K − 273.
How does the Sun's energy reach Earth through empty space?
questions.why: Radiation does not need any material; conduction and convection do.

questions.q: A metal spoon is placed in a hot drink and its handle warms up. Which process is this?
questions.why: Energy passes along the solid metal from particle to particle.

questions.q: Match each example to the heat transfer process.
pairs: Warm air rising from a heater
questions.why: Each example shows a different way heat travels.

questions.q: A cup of boiling water (1 kg at 100 °C) and a large pool at 30 °C. Which has the higher temperature and which holds far more thermal energy?
o: The cup is hotter; the pool holds more thermal energy
The pool is hotter and holds more thermal energy
The cup is hotter and holds more thermal energy
They have equal temperature and equal energy
questions.why: Temperature is average particle energy; total thermal energy also depends on how many particles there are.

questions.q: Order these from lowest to highest temperature.
questions.why: The values increase in this order.

questions.q: Why do we use wooden or plastic handles on cooking pots?
questions.model: Wood and plastic are poor conductors, so heat does not flow easily to the handle and our hands stay safe, unlike with a metal handle.
questions.why: Insulators reduce conduction.

questions.q: Why are the heating coils of a room heater usually near the bottom of the heater and not the top?
o: Warm air rises, setting up a convection current
Heat cannot move upwards through the air at all
The floor needs most of the heat to stay warm
The heavy coils would fall off higher up
questions.why: Warm air rises and cool air sinks, so heating from below mixes the air in the room.

panel.q: On a hot day a white car stays cooler inside than a black car. Which explanation is best?
o: White surfaces reflect more radiation and absorb less
White metal is thicker and so cools better
Black paint makes extra sunshine for the car
White paint cools the engine from outside
panel.why: Dark surfaces absorb more radiant energy, while light surfaces reflect more.

panel.q: Why does a thermos flask keep drinks hot for hours? Mention at least two ideas.
panel.model: A vacuum gap between the walls stops conduction and convection, shiny surfaces reflect radiation, and a stopper reduces loss from the top.
panel.why: Each feature blocks one heat-transfer path.

panel.q: A student says: 'Ice cubes have no heat energy.' What is the best reply?
o: Ice still has thermal energy, just less than warmer water
She is right, ice has no thermal energy at all
Ice has only cold energy, not heat energy
Heat energy needs light to exist
panel.why: Particles in ice still vibrate. Heat flows from warmer things into ice and melts it.

teach.topic: The difference between heat and temperature and how heat travels
teach.model: Temperature tells how hot something is. Heat is energy moving from a hotter place to a colder one. Heat travels by conduction through touch, by convection in moving liquids and gases, and by radiation through space. For example, the Sun warms Earth by radiation.

points.ask: What does temperature tell us?
What is heat then?
How does heat move through solids?
What about through liquids, air and space?

stages.title: Waves, sound and light
stages.hook: You see a lightning flash and hear thunder a few seconds later. Why do they not arrive together?
explain: A wave transfers energy without carrying matter along. Wavelength (λ) is the distance between two matching points, and frequency (f) is the number of waves per second, in hertz (Hz). The wave speed is v = f × λ.

Sound is a longitudinal wave: air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel. It needs a material to travel through and moves at about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C. Higher frequency means higher pitch, and bigger amplitude means louder sound.

Light is an electromagnetic wave. It needs no material and travels at about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, about a million times faster than sound in air. Light reflects from mirrors and bends (refracts) when it moves between materials such as air and water.

example.q: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?

analogies.sea: Sea waves lift a floating boat up and down but do not carry it to the shore by themselves.
analogies.music: A guitar string vibrating faster makes a higher note.
analogies.sport: A crowd doing a 'wave' in a stadium passes along while people stay in their seats.
analogies.nature: Ripples spread out from a stone dropped in a pond.

stages.mnemonic: Waves carry energy, not stuff; v = f λ.
terms: Distance between two matching points on a wave.
Number of waves per second, in hertz.
The maximum displacement of a wave from rest.
A wave bouncing off a surface.

misc.wrong: Sound can travel through empty space like light.
misc.right: Sound needs a material. Light and other electromagnetic waves can cross a vacuum.

stages.limits: Light also behaves like particles, called photons, in some experiments. The wave model is enough for reflection and refraction here.

trip.prompt: Find animations of a transverse and a longitudinal wave.

questions.q: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.why: Frequency counts waves per second, in hertz (Hz).

questions.q: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6 m. What is its speed?
Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is lightning if the thunder arrives 3 s after the flash? Ignore light's travel time.
questions.why: distance = 340 × 3 = 1020 m.

questions.q: A sound wave has speed 340 m/s and frequency 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
Which wave can travel through a vacuum?
questions.why: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium.

questions.q: A sound gets higher in pitch. What has increased?
questions.why: Pitch rises with frequency.

questions.q: Match each wave property to what it changes in sound.
questions.why: Higher frequency sounds higher; larger amplitude sounds louder.

questions.q: Put these in order from slowest to fastest speed.
questions.why: Sound is slower in air than in solids like steel, and light is by far the fastest.

questions.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
questions.model: Light travels much faster than sound, so the flash reaches us almost instantly while the sound of thunder takes several seconds.
questions.why: Light moves at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, sound at about 343 m/s.

questions.q: A boy shouts toward a cliff and hears an echo 2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far is the cliff?
questions.why: The sound travels there and back in 2 s, so total distance = 680 m, one way 340 m.

panel.q: Two astronauts on the Moon are not near any radio. Can they talk by shouting without helmets touching?
o: No, there is no air for sound to travel through
Yes, because sound is a kind of light wave
Yes, if they shout loudly enough to be heard
Yes, but only low sounds can cross space
panel.why: Sound needs a medium. The Moon has almost no atmosphere.

panel.q: A wave on a rope moves to the right. Explain whether the rope itself travels to the right.
panel.model: No. The wave carries energy along the rope, but each piece of rope only moves up and down about its rest position.
panel.why: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter.

panel.q: A straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water. What is the cause?
o: Light changes direction (refracts) as it passes between water and air
The straw is bent by the weight of the water
The glass magnifies the sound of the straw
The cold water softens and bends the straw
panel.why: Light changes speed and direction at the boundary, a process called refraction.

teach.topic: What a wave is and how sound differs from light
teach.model: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the material along. Its speed equals frequency times wavelength. Sound needs air or another material and travels at about 343 m/s. Light does not need anything and is far faster, so we see lightning before we hear thunder.

points.ask: What does a wave carry?
How do speed, frequency and wavelength link up?
What does sound need to travel?
And how is light different?

stages.title: Solar System structure and Moon phases
stages.hook: The Moon seems to change shape every night, from a thin curve to a full circle. Does the Moon really change shape?
explain: Our Solar System has one star, the Sun, and eight planets. The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. The four outer planets are Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants), and Uranus and Neptune (ice giants). Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, and dwarf planets such as Pluto lie beyond Neptune.

The Moon orbits Earth about once every 27.3 days, and the cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. The Moon makes no light; we see the half that the Sun lights. As the Moon orbits, we see different amounts of that bright half.

The phases go: new Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full Moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent, then new again. At full Moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon. At new Moon, the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun and its lit side faces away from us.

example.q: Which Moon phase do we see when the Moon is on the same side of Earth as the Sun?
steps: The Sun lights the half of the Moon that faces the Sun.
That half faces away from Earth.
So we see almost none of the lit side.

analogies.home: Shine a torch on a ball in a dark room and walk around it: you see different amounts of the lit half.
analogies.sport: A runner on a track passes a camera at different angles, but the stadium never changes.
analogies.nature: A pebble in a sunbeam looks lit on one side and dark on the other.
analogies.tech: A phone camera flash lights only the side of an object facing it.

stages.mnemonic: The Moon is always half-lit; we only see how much of that half faces us.
terms: The curved path of one body around another.
How much of the Moon's lit side we see.
A region of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter.
A large planet made mainly of hydrogen and helium.

misc.wrong: Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow on the Moon.
misc.right: Phases come from our changing view of the Moon's lit half. Earth's shadow causes only lunar eclipses.

stages.limits: Planet sizes and distances are hard to draw to scale: if the Sun were a football, Earth would be a pea about 25 m away.

trip.prompt: Find the diagram with the Sun, Earth and the Moon in eight positions.

questions.q: How many planets are in the Solar System?
questions.why: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.q: Which planet is the largest in the Solar System?
questions.why: Jupiter is the largest planet.

questions.q: What lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter?
questions.why: The main asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.q: Order the inner planets by distance from the Sun, nearest first.
questions.why: That is their order from the Sun.

questions.q: Match each Moon phase to what we see.
pairs: Almost none of the lit side
questions.why: These are three main phases.

questions.q: About how many days pass from one full Moon to the next?
questions.why: The cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.

questions.q: It is a full Moon. Where is the Moon compared with the Sun and Earth?
o: On the opposite side of Earth from the Sun
Between Earth and the Sun, in a straight line
questions.why: At full Moon we see the whole lit face, so Earth is roughly between the Sun and the Moon.

questions.q: A friend says phases happen because Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon. Explain why this is wrong.
questions.model: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. Phases happen because, as the Moon orbits Earth, we view different amounts of that lit half. Earth's shadow only causes a lunar eclipse, which is rare.
questions.why: Phases come from viewing geometry, not Earth's shadow.

questions.q: A crescent Moon appears low in the evening sky just after sunset. Which phase is it more likely to be?
questions.why: A waxing crescent is east of the Sun, so it sets shortly after the Sun in the evening.

questions.q: Which statement about the inner planets is correct?
o: They have ring systems like Saturn
questions.why: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky.

panel.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon from Earth?
o: The Moon rotates once for each orbit
The Moon does not rotate or move
The other side is made of different rock
panel.why: The Moon is tidally locked: its rotation period equals its orbital period, about 27.3 days.

panel.q: Why is there not a lunar eclipse at every full Moon?
panel.model: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees from Earth's orbit, so most full Moons pass above or below Earth's shadow. Only when they line up exactly does an eclipse occur.
panel.why: The tilt of the orbit prevents alignment most months.

panel.q: A year on a planet is one orbit of the Sun. Why is a year on Neptune far longer than on Earth?
o: Neptune is much farther away, so its path is longer and it moves slower
Neptune is much smaller than Earth, so it turns more slowly
Neptune has no atmosphere to slow it down
Neptune spins on its axis faster than Earth does
panel.why: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years because its orbit is huge and its speed is lower.

teach.model: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half, so it looks like it changes shape. A full cycle takes about 29.5 days. For example, at full Moon we see the whole lit face.

points.ask: Where does the Moon's light come from?
What does the Moon do over a month?
So why does it look different each night?
Can you name some phases or give an example?
